pearls.label: CPAP = non-invasive, PEEP = invasive
pearls.insight: CPAP refers to continuous positive airway pressure delivered non-invasively via a face mask, while PEEP refers to the same continuous-pressure concept applied through an invasive ventilator circuit with an endotracheal tube.

pearls.label: CPAP/PEEP delivers constant pressure
pearls.insight: In CPAP/PEEP, you dial in a pressure rather than a volume. That pressure stays the same whether the patient is breathing in or out, maintaining airway pressure throughout the respiratory cycle.

pearls.label: PEEP keeps alveoli open (recruited)
pearls.insight: Positive end-expiratory pressure keeps small airways and alveolar clusters open at the end of exhalation, a process called recruitment, rather than letting them collapse to zero pressure. Higher PEEP recruits more alveoli and therefore improves oxygenation.

pearls.label: Pressure support is a key weaning mode
pearls.insight: Pressure support delivers a set pressure with each patient-triggered breath; higher pressure yields larger breaths. It is a popular mode for weaning patients off the ventilator.

pearls.label: Rate+Vt affect CO₂; FiO₂+PEEP affect O₂
pearls.insight: The first two AC ventilator parameters—backup rate and tidal volume—determine minute ventilation and thus CO₂ removal. The last two—FiO₂ and PEEP—primarily determine oxygenation.

pearls.label: Negative deflection marks patient-triggered breath
pearls.insight: A patient-triggered breath shows a negative pressure deflection on the waveform; a ventilator-triggered (backup rate) breath lacks this negative deflection but otherwise looks the same.

pearls.label: AC mode: volume set, pressure variable
pearls.insight: In AC mode the clinician dials in tidal volume; the resulting pressure is variable and depends on lung compliance. Decreased compliance (e.g., pulmonary edema, pneumothorax) yields higher pressure for the same volume.

pearls.label: Peak vs plateau pressure distinction ahead
pearls.insight: There are two types of pressures to be concerned about in mechanical ventilation: peak pressure and plateau pressure. This distinction will be covered in the next lecture.

concepts.title: CPAP vs PEEP terminology
concepts.summary: CPAP is the term used when continuous positive pressure is delivered non-invasively via a mask; PEEP is the term for the same concept delivered through an invasive ventilator with an endotracheal tube.
concepts.body: The speaker clarifies that the term 'CPAP' is typically used when the continuous-pressure mode is non-invasive—i.e., delivered through a face mask (like a CPAP or BiPAP mask) rather than an endotracheal tube. When the same continuous-pressure concept is used on an intubated patient connected to a ventilator, it is referred to as 'PEEP.' Both are essentially the same mode of ventilation.

concepts.title: Continuous pressure in CPAP/PEEP
concepts.summary: CPAP/PEEP delivers a set continuous pressure that remains the same during inspiration and exhalation; you dial in a pressure rather than a volume or rate.
concepts.body: In CPAP/PEEP mode, the clinician dials in a continuous pressure rather than a specific volume or vent setting. The pressure does not change whether the patient is breathing in or breathing out—they always receive the same amount of pressure. PEEP stands for 'positive end-expiratory pressure,' meaning that even at the very end of exhalation, there is still pressure left in the airways (e.g., if set to 5, there is still a pressure of 5 cm H₂O in the airways at end-exhalation instead of zero).

concepts.title: CPAP and PEEP setting range
concepts.summary: CPAP and PEEP can each be set anywhere from 5 to 20 cm of water pressure.
concepts.body: The speaker states that CPAP can be set anywhere from 5 cm of water pressure up to 20, and PEEP can similarly be set from 5 to 20 cm H₂O. These pressures are present on both inspiration and exhalation.

concepts.title: PEEP alveolar recruitment
concepts.summary: PEEP keeps small distal airways and alveolar clusters open and recruited at end-exhalation, preventing collapse to zero pressure.
concepts.body: In invasive ventilation, the airways narrow down to tiny passages ending in grape-like clusters (alveoli). PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is effective at keeping those alveoli open and 'recruited.' To recruit more alveoli, the clinician can increase the PEEP setting on the ventilator, typically via its own dedicated dial.

concepts.title: CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea
concepts.summary: In non-invasive mode, CPAP helps obstructive sleep apnea by keeping airway pressure high enough to hold the tongue forward and keep the airway open.
concepts.body: The speaker explains that in non-invasive mode, CPAP is beneficial for patients with obstructive sleep apnea because the continuous pressure in the airway keeps the tongue forward and maintains an open airway, preventing obstruction during sleep.

concepts.title: Pressure support ventilation
concepts.summary: Pressure support (PS) delivers a set pressure with each patient-triggered breath—unlike pressure control, you cannot set a rate. Higher pressure yields a larger breath. PS is a popular weaning mode.
concepts.body: Pressure support is similar to PEEP/CPAP but is delivered only on patient-initiated breaths. It is also like AC (assist control) except that instead of delivering a specific volume, it delivers a specific pressure support for each breath. The patient initiates all breaths; unlike pressure control, you cannot set a rate. Higher pressure support results in bigger breaths. Pressure support is a very popular weaning mode of ventilation.

concepts.title: Pressure support range
concepts.summary: Pressure support can be set anywhere from 5 to 15 (cm H₂O).
concepts.body: The speaker states that the specific amount of pressure delivered per breath in pressure support ventilation can be anywhere from 5 to 15.

concepts.title: Four ventilation modes compared
concepts.summary: The four modes discussed are AC (volume-based, patient-triggered with backup rate), pressure control (pressure-based, settable rate), CPAP (continuous pressure regardless of breathing phase), and pressure support (patient-triggered, pressure per breath).
concepts.body: The speaker reviews four ventilator modes covered so far: AC, pressure control, CPAP, and pressure support. Each mode differs in whether it targets volume or pressure, whether the patient or ventilator initiates breaths, and whether a rate can be set.

concepts.title: Writing AC mode ventilator orders
concepts.summary: To write AC mode ventilator orders you specify: (1) mode + backup rate, (2) tidal volume, (3) FiO₂, and (4) PEEP. AC is the most common mode in a medical ICU.
concepts.body:
The speaker outlines four things to specify when writing ventilator orders in AC mode:

1. **Mode** — e.g., AC (assist control continuous mandatory ventilation). Whenever the patient triggers the ventilator they get a set volume. You also set a **backup rate** (e.g., 16 breaths/min) so the ventilator guarantees at least that many breaths even if the patient does not breathe.
2. **Tidal volume** — e.g., 550 mL per breath.
3. **FiO₂** — fractional inspired oxygen (e.g., 50%), meaning the percentage of the delivered gas that is oxygen.
4. **PEEP** — e.g., 5 cm H₂O, to keep alveoli recruited.

AC is described as the most common mode of ventilation seen in a medical intensive care unit.

concepts.title: Vent parameters and gas exchange
concepts.summary: The first two AC parameters (backup rate and tidal volume) determine minute ventilation and therefore affect CO₂ removal; the last two (FiO₂ and PEEP) primarily affect oxygenation.
concepts.body: The speaker explains that the four AC ventilator parameters divide into two functional pairs. The backup rate and tidal volume together determine minute ventilation (how much air is moved per minute), which controls CO₂ clearance. The FiO₂ (amount of oxygen delivered) and PEEP (higher PEEP recruits more alveoli) primarily determine oxygenation. Clinicians can manipulate these values to achieve the desired blood gas results.

concepts.title: PEEP recruits alveoli for oxygenation
concepts.summary: PEEP is the pressure left in the circuit at the end of exhalation, present to recruit alveoli. Higher PEEP recruits more alveoli and improves oxygenation.
concepts.body: At the end of exhalation, PEEP leaves a set amount of pressure in the circuit. This pressure is there to recruit alveoli. The higher the PEEP, the more alveoli can be recruited, and therefore the better the oxygenation will be. PEEP is one of the two parameters that primarily affects oxygenation (the other being FiO2).

concepts.title: Ventilator parameter effects on gas exchange
concepts.summary: The four key ventilator parameters split into two functional groups: rate and tidal volume affect CO2 (through minute ventilation), while FiO2 and PEEP affect oxygenation.
concepts.body: The ventilator parameters can be divided by their primary effect on blood gases. The first two parameters — rate (how fast the patient breathes) and tidal volume (how much breath per breath) — affect carbon dioxide by determining minute ventilation. The last two parameters — FiO2 and PEEP — affect oxygenation. These values can be manipulated to achieve the desired effect on the blood gas.

concepts.title: AC mode example ventilator settings
concepts.summary: Example AC mode settings used for the waveform discussion: rate 16, tidal volume 550, FiO2 50%, PEEP 5.
concepts.body: The speaker uses specific settings to illustrate AC mode: AC rate of 16, tidal volume of 550, FiO2 of 50%, and a PEEP of 5. These settings are used to walk through the pressure-volume-flow waveform analysis.

concepts.title: AC mode breath cycle on waveforms
concepts.summary: In AC mode a patient-triggered breath starts with negative pressure deflection, triggering the ventilator to deliver preset tidal volume at constant flow; pressure rises to a peak, then during exhalation everything returns to baseline with pressure stopping at PEEP (not zero).
concepts.body: With a PEEP of 5, there is always pressure in the circuit. When the patient takes a breath, pressure drops to negative, triggering the ventilator to deliver the preset tidal volume. Volume goes up to the preset level while flow enters the lung at a constant preset rate. As volume enters, pressure rises to a maximum. Once the preset tidal volume is reached, flow stops and reverses — flow comes back out of the patient. Pressure falls back down but does not go to zero because PEEP of 5 remains. Volume returns to zero. The cycle repeats with the next breath. Flow rate can be set separately (though not among the four main settings), which is important when ventilating COPD patients.

concepts.title: Triggered vs backup breath on pressure waveform
concepts.summary: A patient-triggered breath shows a negative deflection in the pressure waveform; a ventilator-triggered (backup rate) breath lacks this negative deflection but otherwise looks the same.
concepts.body: When a patient triggers a breath (e.g., an alert patient initiating inspiration), you will see a negative deflection in the pressure tracing before the ventilator delivers the breath. When the ventilator delivers a breath due to the backup rate (e.g., an overly sedated patient who does not trigger), there is no negative deflection — you just see pressure go up. Everything else on the ventilator waveform looks the same for both types of breaths.

concepts.title: AC mode: volume set, pressure variable
concepts.summary: In AC mode the clinician dials in the tidal volume; the pressure is variable and depends on lung compliance. Decreased compliance (e.g., pulmonary edema, pneumothorax) results in higher pressure for the same delivered volume.
concepts.body: In AC mode of ventilation, the clinician sets a preset tidal volume. The ventilator will always deliver that same volume regardless of compliance. However, if the compliance of the system goes down — as with pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, or anything preventing the lung from expanding as easily as it would normally — the ventilator still delivers the same volume but at a higher pressure. That higher pressure is a result of decreased compliance in the lung. So in AC mode: volume is set, pressure is variable depending on compliance.

concepts.title: Pressure alarm for decreased compliance
concepts.summary: A pressure alarm can be set so that if lung compliance decreases and pressure exceeds the threshold, a bell alerts the nurse or respiratory therapist to the problem.
concepts.body: Because pressure varies with compliance in AC mode, you can set a pressure alarm on the ventilator. If the compliance of the lung goes down (e.g., pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, or anything preventing normal lung expansion) and the resulting pressure exceeds the set alarm threshold, a bell will go off. This draws the respiratory therapist or nurse to the bedside because there is a problem requiring attention.

concepts.title: Peak and plateau pressures
concepts.summary: There are two types of pressures to be concerned about in mechanical ventilation: peak pressure and plateau pressure.
concepts.body: The speaker notes that there are actually two types of pressures to be concerned about in mechanical ventilation — peak pressure and plateau pressure. This distinction will be discussed in the next lecture.

themes.title: Positive pressure fundamentals: CPAP, PEEP, and alveolar recruitment
themes.body: CPAP and PEEP both deliver continuous positive pressure throughout the respiratory cycle—the distinction is delivery route (non-invasive mask vs invasive circuit). PEEP's key physiologic role is alveolar recruitment: keeping small airways and alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration, which directly improves oxygenation.

themes.title: Ventilator parameters map to specific gas-exchange goals
themes.body: The four primary AC ventilator settings divide cleanly along physiologic lines: rate and tidal volume govern minute ventilation and therefore CO₂ removal, while FiO₂ and PEEP govern oxygenation. This framework lets clinicians target the correct parameter for the blood-gas abnormality they want to correct.

themes.title: Volume-controlled vs pressure-controlled thinking
themes.body: AC mode fixes tidal volume and lets airway pressure vary with lung compliance—stiffer lungs produce higher pressures. CPAP/PEEP and pressure support instead fix a pressure target and let volume be the dependent variable. Recognizing which variable is held constant is essential for understanding each mode's behavior and monitoring requirements.

themes.title: Waveforms reveal patient effort and ventilator response
themes.body: Pressure waveforms provide visual confirmation of whether a breath was patient-triggered (negative deflection preceding the breath) or machine-triggered (no negative deflection). This connects ventilator mode settings to observable bedside data and helps assess patient-ventilator interaction.
